body.text: In Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) programme, trial and error alone does not qualify under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Claimants must show a systematic investigation: hypotheses targeting technological uncertainty, testing by experiment or analysis, and contemporaneous records. The Tax Court rejected shop-floor trial-and-error tests in Joel Theatrical Rigging for failing the scientific method.

This report provides an exhaustive legal, technical, and financial reference on the research and development (R&D) tax incentives, direct innovation grants, administrative compliance procedures, and judicial precedents of Canada as of late 2026.

Canada operates one of the world's most comprehensive R&D fiscal regimes, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program under the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (ITA) and the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945. The federal programme delivers two statutory incentives: first, an immediate 100% income tax deduction against business income (with indefinite carryforward of unused pool balances) via a dedicated expenditure pool under Section 37 of the ITA; and second, an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA ranging from a 15% basic rate to an enhanced 35% refundable rate, with unused non-refundable credits carrying back 3 taxation years and forward 20 taxation years.

Between December 2024 and late 2026, Canada's R&D tax architecture underwent its most significant statutory expansion in over a decade. Enacted via Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026 and applies retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and to capital property acquired or lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024), Parliament doubled the expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $6 million (yielding up to $2.1 million in annual refundable federal credits), widened the taxable capital phase-out corridor from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, introduced an elective 3-year average gross revenue phase-out test, extended the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for the first time, and restored the eligibility of depreciable capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs. Subsequently, the CRA launched the optional 8-week Pre-Claim Approval Process announced in Budget 2025 on April 1, 2026, and Federal Budget 2026 proposed a $930 million SR&ED commercialisation expansion covering regulatory certification testing and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs, alongside the proposed permanent $36 billion Productivity Mega Deduction. Concurrently, provincial regimes have evolved rapidly, highlighted by Québec's replacement of eight legacy R&D tax measures with the unified 30%/20% refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, British Columbia's permanent extension and expansion of its 10% SR&ED credit to ECPCs and the $6 million limit, and Saskatchewan's doubling of its refundable CCPC cap to $2 million.
1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Regime

The Canadian federal SR&ED programme is not a discretionary grant application; it is a statutory entitlement codified within the Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Regulations. Where a taxpayer's technical activities satisfy the statutory definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1) and the associated expenditures meet the timing, substantiation, and prescribed form-filing requirements of Sections 37 and 127, the Minister of National Revenue is legally required to allow the deduction and issue the resulting Investment Tax Credits. Because the statutory mechanics are distributed across multiple interlocking sections of the ITA and Parts XI, XXIX, and XLVI of the Regulations, precise statutory mapping is essential for compliance and audit defence.
1.1 Core Provisions of the Federal Income Tax Act (ITA)

The statutory foundation of every SR&ED claim begins in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, which houses the legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development". Subsection 248(1) structures eligible work into three primary research categories—basic research under paragraph (a), applied research under paragraph (b), and experimental development under paragraph (c)—together with eight enumerated categories of eligible support work under paragraph (d) and seven mandatory statutory exclusions under paragraphs (e) through (k). Subsection 248(1) also provides the statutory definitions of "salary or wages", "specified employee", and "salary deferral arrangement", which govern payroll eligibility and proxy overhead calculations across the Act.

Once work satisfies subsection 248(1), subsection 37(1) of the ITA establishes a cumulative, non-expiring pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada and related to a business of the taxpayer. Taxpayers may deduct any portion of this pool in computing business income in the current taxation year or carry the undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to reduce taxable business income in future taxation years. Within subsection 37(1), paragraph 37(1)(a) governs expenditures of a current nature, subdivided into five specific streams: subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) covers current expenditures on SR&ED directly undertaken by the taxpayer; subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) covers current expenditures for SR&ED directly undertaken on behalf of the taxpayer by arm's-length or non-arm's-length subcontractors; subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1) covers third-party payments made to a corporation resident in Canada (an "A Entity") to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to a business of the taxpayer where the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results; subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii) covers third-party payments made to approved associations ("B Entities"), approved universities, colleges, or research institutes ("C Entities"), non-profit SR&ED corporations exempt from tax under paragraph 149(1)(j) ("D Entities"), or approved granting councils under clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(E) ("E Entities"); and subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii) covers payments by a corporation to a tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporation ("F Entity") for basic or applied research.

Complementing current expenditures, paragraph 37(1)(b)—enacted by Bill C-15 for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024—restores the eligibility of expenditures of a capital nature made by the taxpayer on SR&ED carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer and related to the taxpayer's business, in respect of property acquired that would otherwise be depreciable property of the taxpayer (other than land or a leasehold interest in land). Paragraph 37(1)(d) requires that the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool be reduced by the total amount of any government assistance or non-government assistance (as defined in subsection 127(9)) in respect of an expenditure described in paragraph 37(1)(a) or 37(1)(b) that, at the taxpayer's filing-due date for the year, the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive.

Several ancillary subsections in Section 37 regulate timing, geographic scope, depreciation integration, overhead elections, and filing deadlines. Subsection 37(1.2) defers the inclusion of capital expenditures until the taxation year in which the depreciable property becomes available for use under subsection 13(27). Subsection 37(2) governs research carried on outside Canada, permitting a current-year income tax deduction for foreign SR&ED expenditures (including foreign contractor costs) when calculating net income or loss, but excluding those amounts from the subsection 37(1) pool and from earning Investment Tax Credits. By contrast, subsection 37(1.4) permits permissible salary or wages paid to Canadian-resident employees directly performing SR&ED outside Canada to be included in the subsection 37(1) pool, though no associated foreign overhead or travel costs may be claimed. Under subsection 37(6), any amount claimed under subsection 37(1) in respect of capital property described in paragraph 37(1)(b) is deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed under paragraph 20(1)(a) as a separate prescribed class for recapture purposes under section 13. Under subsection 37(6.1) (specifically clause 37(6.1)(a)(i)(B)), a loss restriction event (such as an acquisition of control of a corporation) restricts the carryforward of unused Section 37 pool balances.

Subsection 37(8) establishes the interpretive rules for what expenditures qualify under the two overhead calculation methods. Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) governs the Traditional Method, encompassing current expenditures all or substantially all (ASA, defined as 90% or more) attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED or the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for SR&ED in Canada (subclause (I)), current expenditures directly attributable to SR&ED as prescribed by Regulations 2900(2) and 2900(3) (subclause (II)), and capital expenditures where at the time incurred it was intended that the property would be used during ASA of its operating time in its expected useful life for—or have ASA of its value consumed in—the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (subclause (III)). Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) governs the Proxy Method, restricting pool inclusions to: (I) current expenditures ASA attributable to the lease of premises, facilities, or equipment for SR&ED in Canada, other than general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF); (II) expenditures for SR&ED directly undertaken on behalf of the taxpayer (contracts); (III) capital expenditures described in subclause (A)(III), other than GPOEF; (IV) salary or wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada; (V) the cost of materials consumed or transformed in SR&ED; and (VI) one-half (50%) of any other current expenditure in respect of the lease of premises, facilities, or equipment used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, other than GPOEF. Paragraphs 37(8)(d) and 37(8)(e) explicitly exclude capital expenditures for acquiring a building or leasehold interest in a building (other than a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 2903) and outlays or expenses made for the use of, or right to use (rent), a building.

Rounding out Section 37, subsection 37(9) prohibits claiming remuneration based on profits or bonuses paid to a specified employee; subsection 37(10) requires the election to use the Proxy Method to be made at the time of filing Form T661, rendering the choice irrevocable for the taxation year; subsection 37(11) establishes the strict 12-month post-filing-due-date reporting deadline for identifying SR&ED expenditures on Form T661; and subsection 37(13) deems support work performed by a non-arm's-length contractor to be SR&ED where the work would have been SR&ED if performed directly by the payer (subsections 37(14) and 37(15), the former capital look-through rules, were repealed by Bill C-15 consequential on the restoration of capital expenditures).

The Investment Tax Credit and its refundability are governed by Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA. Subsection 127(5) authorizes the deduction of earned SR&ED ITCs against Part I federal tax otherwise payable, while subsection 127(8) governs the allocation of partnership ITCs to partners. Subsection 127(9) contains the core ITC definitions, including "investment tax credit" (fixing the 15% basic rate, the 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward periods, and paragraph (m), which imposes the 12-month post-filing-due-date reporting deadline for Schedule T2SCH31 and Form T2038(IND)), "qualified expenditure" (including the 80% inclusion rule for arm's-length contracts and third-party payments under paragraph (g), the Prescribed Proxy Amount [PPA], and restored First-Term and Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment [SUE] under paragraph (a)(iii) and paragraph (c)), "contract payment", "government assistance", "non-government assistance", "consolidated financial statements", and "eligible Canadian public corporation". Subsections 127(10.1) to 127(10.6) govern the additional 20% ITC enhancement (creating the 35% enhanced rate) and the calculation, phase-out, and allocation of the expenditure limit for CCPCs and ECPCs. Subsections 127(11.1) to 127(20) govern assistance reductions (subsection 127(18)), non-arm's length transfers (subsection 127(13)), and non-arm's length capital/expenditure cost adjustments (paragraph 127(11.5)(b) and subsection 127(11.6), reintroduced effective December 16, 2024). Subsection 127(26) enforces the 180-day unpaid amount rule for non-salary current expenditures, and subsections 127(27) to 127(36) govern the 20-year ITC recapture regime. Finally, subsections 127.1(1), 127.1(2), and 127.1(2.01) establish the Refundable Investment Tax Credit (RITC) mechanics and the "qualifying income limit".

Tax practitioners, corporate controllers, and auditors reviewing claims in 2026 and beyond must account for two distinct waves of legislative reform: first, the major structural expansion proposed in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) and Budget 2025, which became law when Bill C-15 received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026; and second, the commercialisation, intellectual property protection, and capital expensing reforms proposed in Federal Budget 2026.

body.text: 2.2 Federal Budget 2026 Proposals (Commercialisation, IP Protection, and the Productivity Mega Deduction) and the Pre-Claim Approval Process

In Federal Budget 2026, the Government of Canada proposed a second package of structural enhancements designed to support domestic commercialisation and capital investment, projected to provide $930 million in additional SR&ED support over five years ($25 million in 2026–27, $200 million in 2027–28, $245 million in 2028–29, $225 million in 2029–30, and $235 million ongoing starting in 2030–31).

First, for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day in 2026, Budget 2026 proposes to expand eligible SR&ED activities to cover regulatory and certification testing requirements—specifically tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements necessary for obtaining initial approval or certification to commercialise a new or improved product or process. To qualify, these validation activities must directly relate to a project that is eligible under existing SR&ED programme rules, and they would attract the same expenditure categories (wages and salaries, materials, contracting costs, overhead costs, and machinery and equipment). The CRA will issue sector-specific guidance to clarify eligibility boundaries for commercialisation expenses.

Second, following the intellectual property performance review announced in Budget 2025, Budget 2026 proposes to expand eligible SR&ED expenditures (for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day) to include Intellectual Property (IP) protection expenditures—specifically expenses reasonably incurred to prepare and file applications for registration, as well as periodic maintenance fees to keep IP rights in force, for IP developed during an eligible SR&ED project. Eligible IP types would encompass patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software registered or protected under relevant Canadian legislation or equivalent foreign legislation. While administrative filing and maintenance fees paid to foreign IP offices would be eligible, costs for supporting preparation activities (such as drafting applications) would qualify only if conducted in Canada. Litigation or enforcement costs (such as suing for alleged IP infringement) and costs not directly connected to securing and maintaining IP rights would be excluded. Moreover, if a taxpayer subsequently disposes of IP for which SR&ED support was claimed on IP protection costs, recapture rules would apply to claw back the related SR&ED deduction and investment tax credit amounts.

Third, Budget 2026 proposes to streamline corporate tax compliance by eliminating, for elections and agreements made on or after Royal Assent of the enacting legislation, the requirement for corporations to file a certified copy of a board of directors' resolution or formal corporate authorization when making elections regarding transfers of qualified SR&ED expenditures between non-arm's length parties or allocations of wages and salaries of specified SR&ED employees. Complementing this administrative simplification, effective April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the optional upfront Pre-Claim Approval Process via My Business Account, enabling businesses to submit planned R&D projects before work begins or costs are incurred and receive a formal technical eligibility determination within 8 weeks, alongside optional one-on-one information sessions. Refundable claims consisting solely of projects granted pre-claim approval that are selected for an expenditure-only review are processed under an accelerated 90-calendar-day service standard.

Fourth, Budget 2026 confirms the proposed Productivity Mega Deduction (following legislative and regulatory proposals released on September 15, 2026, building on the prior year's Productivity Super Deduction), with an estimated fiscal cost of $36 billion over five years beginning in 2026–27. This measure would permanently allow Canadian businesses to immediately write off 100% of the full cost of a broad range of capital assets—representing more than 65% of business investment across manufacturing, modular housing, construction, farming, agri-food processing, fishing, tourism, health care and medical equipment, transportation, and media production—and would increase the deduction rate for Canadian Development Expenses (CDE) from 30% declining-balance to 100%. Consequently, Canada's Marginal Effective Tax Rate (METR) on new business investment would drop from 13% to 6.4%, the lowest METR in the G7 and less than half the United States rate of 16.9%. Additionally, Budget 2026 proposes to extend both the 15% Mineral Exploration Tax Credit (METC) and the 30% Critical Mineral Exploration Tax Credit (CMETC) (expanded to include antimony) for 5 years to flow-through share agreements entered into on or before March 31, 2032 ($956 million over 5 years), and to extend 100% Canadian Exploration Expense (CEE) and CDE treatment to helium exploration and development expenses incurred on or after Budget Day ($54 million through 2030–31).
3. Technical Eligibility Framework: Statutory Definitions, CRA Guidelines, and the Common-Law Test

Determining whether work constitutes SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act is the threshold question of every claim. Section 127 and Section 37 only determine how qualified expenditures are quantified once technical eligibility under subsection 248(1) is established.
3.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED (ITA Subsection 248(1))

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, "scientific research and experimental development" is defined as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. This overarching requirement applies to three core categories of research: basic research under paragraph (a), defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; applied research under paragraph (b), defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and experimental development under paragraph (c), defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. In commercial practice, experimental development is where nearly all industry and software SR&ED claims reside.

Once core research under paragraph (a), (b), or (c) is established, paragraph 248(1)(d) brings support work within the meaning of SR&ED where the work is undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to one of eight strictly enumerated technical disciplines: (1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, or (8) psychological research. Work in these eight categories never constitutes SR&ED on its own. To qualify under paragraph (d), the support work must satisfy two cumulative statutory conditions: first, it must be commensurate with the needs (corresponding strictly in amount, size, extent, or duration to what is necessary to carry out the basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada); and second, it must be directly in support of that basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada.
Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) establish seven mandatory statutory exclusions, declaring that SR&ED does not include work with respect to:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion;
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities;
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas;
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
Paragraph (j): Style changes; or
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection.

body.text: As detailed in CRA policy, these exclusions are evaluated in Step 2 (determining the extent of eligible work) only after Step 1 has established that core SR&ED exists. The presence of an excluded activity within a broader commercial venture (for example, mineral prospecting in a mining technology project) does not automatically taint or disqualify the entire project; rather, paragraphs (d) and (e)–(k) delineate the boundary between eligible SR&ED support work and ineligible commercial work based on purpose—specifically, why the activity was performed.
3.2 Evolution and Reconciliation: The Five Northwest Hydraulic Questions vs. The CRA's 2021 "Why" and "How" Guidelines

A frequent point of contention in SR&ED reviews and Tax Court appeals is the relationship between the common-law Five Questions established by the Tax Court of Canada and the simplified Two Requirements ("Why" and "How") published by the CRA in August 2021.

Historically, prior to 1985, Revenue Canada administered R&D eligibility under Interpretation Bulletin IT-439. In May 1985, the Department of Finance tabled Budget Papers amending the definition to include "experimental development" while confirming that routine engineering or routine development remained excluded. On March 4, 1986, the Department of Finance confirmed three essential criteria—scientific or technological advancement, scientific or technological uncertainty, and systematic organization—which were codified in Information Circular IC 86-4 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development, revised through IC 86-4R3 in 1994) and clarified by Department of Finance News Release 92-088 on December 2, 1992. In May 1998, in the landmark decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839; [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520; 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC)), Judge Bowman synthesized IC 86-4R3 and subsection 248(1) into a five-question judicial framework. The CRA embedded these five questions in its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (published in 2012, revised April 24, 2015, and archived in August 2021).

In August 2021 (last updated August 13, 2021), as part of its modernization initiative, the CRA replaced the 2015 policy with the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, condensing the self-assessment framework into two overarching requirements: The "Why" Requirement and The "How" Requirement. Crucially, as the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed in National R&D Inc. v. The Queen (2022 FCA 72) and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2021 FCA 88), the statutory text of subsection 248(1) did not change, CRA administrative guidelines are not binding on the courts, and the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain the binding legal test in Canada.

body.text: 3.3 Granular Technical Nuances in CRA Eligibility Reviews

During a technical review by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), claims are evaluated against six well-established doctrinal distinctions in CRA guidelines. First, claimants must distinguish between a technical problem and a technological uncertainty. A technical problem is an operational issue that can be resolved by applying known or openly available practices, techniques, methodologies, or existing vendor solutions—for example, a chemical plant tracing pump corrosion to an upstream filter operating above its design temperature and replacing it with an existing high-temperature filter. Conversely, a technological uncertainty exists when whether a result can be achieved or how to achieve it cannot be determined on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience in the company's business environment—for example, a pump manufacturer whose pumps repeatedly corrode even after replacing shaft seals, creating uncertainty regarding alloy material properties under corrosive parameters or seal profile geometry.

Second, while project size or complexity alone never proves technological uncertainty, system uncertainty arises during the integration of individual components or sub-systems (even where the individual components are well known) due to unpredictable or adverse interactions across component boundaries where overall system performance cannot be predicted. Resolving system uncertainty qualifies as SR&ED when it requires changing or advancing the underlying technologies of the sub-systems rather than merely applying existing integration practices. Third, while commercial objectives or cost targets do not in themselves constitute technological uncertainty, attempting to meet a strict cost target can create technological uncertainty when proven methods (such as using a costly tin oxide and platinum catalyst to convert carbon monoxide to carbon dioxide at room temperature) are economically unviable for commercial production and the alternative chemical or physical pathways to achieve an inexpensive room-temperature process are technologically uncertain.

Fourth, technological advancement is the generation of information or discovery of knowledge that advances the understanding of scientific relations or technology to a higher level. Crucially, advancement can be achieved even when a project fails to meet its commercial or technical objectives: rejecting a hypothesis through systematic testing is itself a technological advancement because it eliminates a possible solution and explains why that approach will not succeed. Fifth, product novelty, innovation, uniqueness, or feature enhancement alone does not establish technological advancement. In the CRA's illustrative "potato peeler" example, systematically testing various phosphorescent powders in a plastic handle to create a novel glow-in-the-dark potato peeler is not SR&ED if adding the powder requires no change to the moulding process or polymer chemistry and does not affect the handle's physical properties.

Sixth, in software engineering, data analytics, and machine learning (ML), reapplying known tools or training established ML models on a company's specific dataset, tuning performance via standard profiling methods, or implementing an existing network protocol does not qualify. Software work qualifies across three core scenarios: (1) where the software itself is the novel object (developing novel algorithms where no known algorithm satisfies performance bounds, designing new storage or indexing architectures to overcome database access-pattern constraints, or creating new ML training methods to resolve known architectural failure modes); (2) where software combined with hardware creates a technologically advanced product (such as embedded control systems with novel signal processing or custom neural networks for specialized hardware); and (3) where custom test frameworks or simulation environments are developed specifically to enable other qualifying SR&ED work.
4. Federal Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Limits, Refundability, and Carryover Rules

Once eligible SR&ED activities are established, the financial value of a federal claim is governed by the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the Section 127 / 127.1 Investment Tax Credit (ITC).
4.1 Federal SR&ED ITC Rates and Refundability Matrix

The federal SR&ED ITC operates on a two-tier rate structure: a basic rate of 15% available to all claimants (corporations, sole proprietorships, partners of a partnership, and trust beneficiaries) under subsection 127(9), and an enhanced rate of 35% (the 15% basic rate plus a 20% addition under subsection 127(10.1)) available to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) on qualified expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit. Any qualified expenditures in excess of the expenditure limit earn an ITC at the basic 15% rate.

Under Section 127.1, any earned ITC must first be applied against federal Part I tax payable for the year; the remaining unused ITC may then be refunded in cash depending on the claimant's legal classification, whether the expenditure falls within or above the expenditure limit, and whether the expenditure is of a current nature (100% refundable at the 35% rate) or a capital nature (40% refundable at the 35% rate for property acquired after December 15, 2024).

body.text: 4.2 Statutory Definitions of CCPC Sub-Categories and ECPCs

To apply the refundability table accurately, four corporate classifications under Sections 125, 127, and 127.1 must be distinguished. First, a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) is defined in subsection 125(7) of the ITA as a private corporation that is a Canadian corporation not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, public corporations, or a combination thereof. Second, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC)—introduced by Bill C-15 in subsection 127(9) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—is a public corporation listed on a designated stock exchange that is resident in Canada and is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner, by one or more non-resident persons (even if all shares owned by non-residents were instead owned by a single hypothetical person, the ECPC would still not be controlled by that person).

Third, under subsection 127.1(2), a Qualifying Corporation is a CCPC whose taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (aggregated across all associated corporations) was not more than its Qualifying Income Limit for the current taxation year. Qualifying corporations (other than excluded corporations) receive not only a 100% refund of the 35% ITC on current expenditures and a 40% refund of the 35% ITC on capital expenditures up to their expenditure limit, but also a 40% refund of the 15% basic ITC earned on current and capital expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit. Fourth, under subsection 127.1(2.01), a CCPC that is neither a qualifying corporation (because its prior-year taxable income exceeded its qualifying income limit) nor an excluded corporation—as well as an ECPC for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—calculates its Refundable Investment Tax Credit using the statutory formula (40% × (A − B)) + (C − D), where A and C account for qualified expenditures and related 35% ITCs on non-capital (current) expenditures up to the expenditure limit, and B and D account for portions deducted against Part I tax under subsections 127(5) and 127(6). This ensures a 100% refund rate on current expenditures and a 40% refund rate on capital expenditures up to the expenditure limit, while any 15% ITC earned above the expenditure limit is non-refundable.
4.3 Mathematical Formulas for the Expenditure Limit and Qualifying Income Limit

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit for both stand-alone CCPCs (or associated CCPC groups) and ECPCs (or consolidated ECPC groups) is $6,000,000 (doubled from the $3,000,000 limit that applied to CCPCs for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024). Under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.21), a CCPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease linearly when the taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and all associated CCPCs) for the immediately preceding taxation year reaches $15,000,000, and becomes nil starting at $75,000,000:

items: Post-December 15, 2024 CCPC Expenditure Limit Formula: Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil (0) if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000.

Pre-December 16, 2024 CCPC Expenditure Limit Formula: Expenditure Limit = $3,000,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000], where A was nil if prior-year taxable capital was $10,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $40,000,000 and the excess over $10,000,000 (eliminated at $50,000,000).

body.text: For Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) under subsection 127(10.6), and for CCPCs that file a revenue election under subsection 127(10.31) (for a single CCPC) or subsection 127(10.32) (jointly across all associated CCPCs), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 is phased out over the exact same $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 band, but using the average annual gross revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years instead of taxable capital. Average annual revenue is determined from the financial statements of all group members (or consolidated financial statements for ECPCs), including a reasonable share of partnership or trust revenue and adjusted for intra-group sales so the revenue reflects a single economic entity (if the entity has fewer than 3 preceding fiscal years, the average is computed over the actual number of fiscal years).
Similarly, to determine whether a CCPC qualifies as a "qualifying corporation", subsection 127.1(2) defines the Qualifying Income Limit for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 as:

items: Qualifying Income Limit Formula: Qualifying Income Limit = $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess over $15,000,000 (replacing the prior $10 million to $50 million phase-out).

If a corporation has a short taxation year (under 51 weeks), or has multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year while associated with another CCPC under subsection 127(10.5), its expenditure limit is prorated by multiplying the limit by the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365.
4.4 Carryback, Carryforward, Recapture, and Acquisition of Control Rules

Under subsection 127(5), any unused non-refundable SR&ED ITC (after reducing current-year federal Part I tax payable to zero and accounting for any cash refund under section 127.1) may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years (applied up to the Part I tax otherwise payable in that prior year) or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years. If the ITC is not applied within the 20-year carryforward window, it expires.

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36), an SR&ED ITC earned on a property (capital equipment, shared-use equipment, or materials transformed into a product or commercial asset) in any of the 20 preceding taxation years is subject to ITC Recapture if the taxpayer disposes of the property or converts it to commercial use. The recaptured amount—which is added directly to Part I federal tax payable—equals the lesser of: (1) the actual SR&ED ITC historically earned on that property, and (2) the historical ITC percentage rate used when the credit was earned multiplied by either the proceeds of disposition (if disposed of to an arm's-length person) or the fair market value of the property (in any other case, such as conversion to commercial use or a non-arm's-length disposition). Special partnership and non-arm's-length allocation recapture rules apply under subsections 127(28), 127(29), 127(32), and 127(33). Crucially, as illustrated in Section 7.1.1 of the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a corporation pays an arm's-length supplier $12,000 under contract to manufacture a custom SR&ED component ($10,000 manufacturing cost plus $2,000 profit), the entire $12,000 cost of the property is subject to recapture upon commercial conversion or sale; conversely, if the same component is manufactured in-house by the claimant, recapture applies only to the raw materials transformed, with no recapture on the in-house salaries or overhead. Finally, when an acquisition of control (loss restriction event) occurs, subsection 37(6.1) and the acquisition-of-control rules in Section 127 restrict the continuity and carryover of both the undeducted Section 37 expenditure pool and unused ITC carryforwards.
5. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Proxy vs. Traditional Overhead Methods, and Cost Rules

To claim SR&ED tax incentives, a taxpayer must link eligible technical work to allowable expenditures incurred during the taxation year across six statutory categories: salaries or wages, materials consumed or transformed, SR&ED contracts, third-party payments, overhead and other expenditures (or the Prescribed Proxy Amount), and restored capital and equipment lease expenditures.
5.1 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, and the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act (reported on a T4 slip), excluding superannuation or pension benefits and retiring allowances. Because dividends paid to founders or shareholders represent distributions of corporate profit rather than employment income subject to T4 source deductions, dividends are completely ineligible for SR&ED claims.

Allowable SR&ED salaries and wages include regular gross wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, regular sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips, honorariums, director's and management fees, commissions, inducement or non-competition payments for employment services, and bonuses or remuneration based on profits paid to employees other than specified employees. Cash outlays for section 6 taxable benefits (such as automobile benefits, housing/board, tuition fees, or group term life insurance) are also includable, and non-cash taxable benefits may be included if: (1) the value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs incurred by the employer, (2) the value excludes GST/HST or PST (unless no input tax credit/refund can be claimed), and (3) the actual costs (including CCA) to which the non-cash benefit relates are not claimed as ordinary business expenses under section 9. Conversely, SR&ED salaries and wages strictly exclude: (1) the employer's share of payroll-related benefits (such as CPP, EI, and health plan contributions, which can only be claimed as overhead under the Traditional Method), (2) extended vacation or extended sick leave (as the employee is not directly engaged in or supporting SR&ED), (3) section 7 employee stock option benefits (which are not an expenditure incurred by the employer), and (4) retiring allowances (which cannot be claimed under the Proxy Method, though they may qualify as overhead under the Traditional Method).

Under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, accrued salary or wages that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred are deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year; instead, they are deemed to be incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid (a payment made on the 180th day is timely). Unpaid wages must be reported on Line 315 of Form T661 in the year accrued in order to be claimed on Line 310 in the future year when paid. Crucially, under Regulation 2900(9), prior-year unpaid wages paid in a current year (Line 310), as well as deemed-paid vacation/holiday pay or salary deferral arrangements unpaid on the 180th day, are excluded from the salary base when calculating the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount.

Special statutory limits apply to any "specified employee"—defined in subsection 248(1) as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a specified shareholder owning, directly or indirectly (including shares owned by non-arm's-length relatives such as a spouse, sibling, or parent), 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation. First, under subsection 37(9), all bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are completely disallowed (unless the employee's only remuneration in the year is a bonus/profit-based amount commensurate with performed SR&ED duties and processed through standard payroll procedures). Second, if a specified employee is employed by associated corporations, each associated corporation must file Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED) by its reporting deadline, or the specified employee's SR&ED salary is deemed nil. Third, under Regulations 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9), the amount of a specified employee's salary that can enter the Salary Base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (calculated on Lines 850–860 of Form T661) is restricted to the lesser of:

body.text: 5.2 Overhead Methodologies: Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method

Under subsection 37(10) of the ITA, a claimant must choose annually on Form T661 between electing the Proxy Method on Line 160 or using the Traditional Method on Line 162 (if no election is made when Form T661 is first filed for the year, the Traditional Method applies automatically). Once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the choice of method is irrevocable for that year.

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not specifically identify or track overhead expenditures on Form T661; instead, actual overhead expenses remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the ITA, and the claimant calculates a notional amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of the eligible Salary Base under Regulation 2900(4) (subject to the overall cap formula A − B − C where A is total net business income deductions including cost of goods sold). As emphasized in CRA policy revisions, the PPA rate has been 55% since 2014 (down from 60% in 2013 and 65% in 2012 and prior years); applying a 65% rate on a 2025 or 2026 filing is a major audit error that overstates the claim by 10 percentage points. The Salary Base (Line 818) includes only the salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (hands-on technical work based on actual tasks performed rather than job title, plus directly engaged technological planning for ongoing projects and supervised machine-operation tasks), reduced on Line 812 by all bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, inducement payments, and prior-year unpaid wages under Regulation 2900(9), and capped for specified employees on Lines 850–860. The resulting 55% PPA (Line 820 / Line 502) earns Investment Tax Credits, but is never included in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool.

Under the Traditional Method, the claimant specifically identifies, tracks, allocates, and documents actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661, adding them to both the Section 37 deductible pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool. Under Regulation 2900(2)(c), every overhead expenditure (or allocated portion thereof) must satisfy two mandatory cumulative tests: first, the Directly Related Test, requiring a direct linkage with no intervening step or intermediary between the expenditure and the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED; and second, the Incremental Test, requiring that the expenditure would not have been incurred had such prosecution of SR&ED not occurred. Fixed monthly telephone, mobile phone, or internet service plans and fixed-cost maintenance contracts fail the incremental test (though identifiable incremental long-distance charges qualify). Direct maintenance and upkeep costs of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment under Regulation 2900(3) are specifically permitted by regulation and do not need to pass the directly related and incremental tests, being allowed in proportion to SR&ED usage.

body.text: 5.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (ITA Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) & (B)(V); Reg. 2900(2)(a))

Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, "materials for SR&ED" refers strictly to physical, tangible raw materials, substances, or items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of a tangible thing on which SR&ED is being carried out or that results from the SR&ED. Materials may be purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers and are claimed at laid-down cost (invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation, acquisition, and storage costs, plus direct labour and production overhead for self-manufactured items, or third-party processing services such as galvanization of metal parts for testing) in the taxation year the material is actually consumed or transformed in Canada.

Two special physical inclusions are recognized in Section 4.0 and Section 7.0 of the Materials for SR&ED Policy: first, in agricultural or biological SR&ED involving animals and growing things, seed, growth media, agar, fungal cultures, animal feed, plant fertilizers, pesticides, herbicides, and fungicides applied to test plots qualify as materials consumed (whereas simultaneous commercial crop production allows only the incremental portion attributable to SR&ED); and second, while general utilities (electricity, natural gas, utility water, boiler feed water) are overhead rather than materials, energy input directly into endothermic reactions (in chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical, biotechnology, metallurgical refining, cement/glass/ceramics, and plastics forming processes where the product physically retains the energy) and process water acting as a chemical feed stream into a product qualify as materials consumed. Conversely, petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes, vials, cleaning products, used engine lubricants, and computer discs/CDs/DVDs do not compose the body of the thing tested and cannot be claimed as materials (qualifying only as Traditional Method overhead).

On Form T661, materials must be segregated between Materials Consumed (Line 320)—materials destroyed or rendered virtually valueless (where 90% or more of the cost is consumed, leaving a resale/scrap value of 10% or less of original cost) as a result of the SR&ED—and Materials Transformed (Line 325), which are materials changed or incorporated into another material, prototype, experimental production run (ED+EP), or commercial asset that retains some value (such as a sale value greater than 10% of original cost, or recycled SR&ED materials). While both are 100% deductible and 100% ITC-eligible in the year of consumption or transformation (provided they are paid within 180 days of year-end under subsection 127(26)), Materials Transformed are subject to the 20-year ITC Recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) if the resulting product or asset is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use.
5.4 Subcontractors (SR&ED Contracts) vs. Third-Party Payments (80% Statutory Inclusion Rule)

Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, both arm's-length contract expenditures for SR&ED performed on behalf of a claimant (Line 340) and third-party payments (Line 370) are subject to the 80% inclusion rule: while 100% of the eligible payment enters the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool, 20% is deducted on Line 529 of Form T661 so that only 80% qualifies to earn Investment Tax Credits.

To claim an SR&ED Contract Expenditure under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), the claimant (payer) must demonstrate that basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible support work (commensurate with and directly supporting the payer's SR&ED) was performed in Canada, related to the payer's business, by a taxable supplier. If a contract combines SR&ED and non-SR&ED work, or work inside and outside Canada, the contract price must be reasonably allocated. During an audit, the CRA evaluates the Master Services Agreement (MSA) and Statement of Work (SOW) to verify that the work was performed "on behalf of" the payer by examining: (1) financial risk (Time-and-Materials billing where the payer pays regardless of technical failure proves the payer bears the risk, whereas fixed-price milestone contracts with strict working-delivery guarantees may make the contractor the rightful SR&ED claimant) and (2) intellectual property ownership (the payer must own the resulting IP or hold an exclusive, unencumbered right to exploit the results). To prevent double-dipping, any "contract payment" received by a Canadian performer from an arm's-length taxable supplier reduces the performer's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under subsection 127(18) (though it does not reduce the performer's Section 37 deductible pool). Conversely, payments made to a non-taxable supplier (such as a foreign contractor) earn zero ITCs for the payer (deducted on Line 528), and payments received by a Canadian performer from a non-taxable foreign client do not constitute a "contract payment", allowing the Canadian performer to claim the full ITCs. For non-arm's-length (NAL) contracts, the payer cannot claim ITCs on the contract payment; instead, under subsection 37(13), support work performed by an NAL contractor is deemed to be SR&ED, enabling the NAL performer to claim the expenditures directly or transfer the qualified expenditures to the NAL payer via Form T1146. Under subsection 127(26), if an arm's-length contract remains unpaid 180 days after year-end, the 80% ITC-eligible portion is deducted on Line 520 (and if not identified on Form T661 within the 18-month reporting deadline, it can never earn an ITC even when paid in a future year on Line 500).

By contrast, Third-Party Payments under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) (reported on Form T1263) are payments made solely for SR&ED in Canada (except specific research chair allocations) where the performer controls the research, there is usually more than one funder, and the claimant obtains a non-exclusive preferential right to exploit the results. The CRA classifies third-party recipients into six entity types: A Entities (corporations resident in Canada under s. 37(1)(a)(i.1), which earn tax incentives only in the year the SR&ED is performed due to subsection 18(9) prepaid expense rules); B Entities (approved associations); C Entities (approved universities, colleges, or research institutes); D Entities (non-profit SR&ED corporations exempt under paragraph 149(1)(j)); E Entities (approved granting councils—CIHR, NSERC, and SSHRC—under clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(E)); and F Entities (exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations under s. 37(1)(a)(iii) for basic or applied research). Payments to B through E entities earn SR&ED incentives on a cash basis in the year paid, and payments in kind to universities or colleges are valued at fair market value.
5.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)
Under Bill C-15, capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024) once again qualify for SR&ED deductions and ITCs.

To qualify as an SR&ED Capital Expenditure under paragraph 37(1)(b) and subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) and (B)(III) (claimed on Line 390 of Form T661), the expenditure must be for the acquisition of depreciable property (owned by the claimant or in which the claimant holds a leasehold interest, available for use after December 15, 2024) where, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended either: (1) to use the property during all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or (2) that ASA (≥90%) of the property's value would be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Land, leasehold interests in land, inventory, goodwill, and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings (other than prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903, though non-building structures or portable shelters may qualify) are excluded. Under the Proxy Method, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF—such as desks, chairs, lamps, photocopiers, and telephones, though computers, hardware, software, and ancillary equipment are not GPOEF) is also excluded. Crucially, while used depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 qualifies for immediate deduction in the Section 37 pool, subparagraph 2902(b)(iii) of the Regulations classifies used property (and refurbishment costs of used property) as a prescribed expenditure that cannot earn an Investment Tax Credit (deducted on Line 532 of Form T661). Capital property claimed on Form T661 is deemed CCA under subsection 37(6) and cannot also be claimed on Schedule 8.

Where new depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 does not meet the ≥90% ASA intent test, is not GPOEF, and is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP under Regulation 2900(11)), it qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under subsection 127(9) if used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada. First-Term SUE requires >50% SR&ED operating use from acquisition (when available for use) to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition, deeming 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (excluding section 21 borrowed money costs and adjusted for non-arm's-length costs under subsection 127(11.6)) to be a qualified expenditure for ITC purposes. If First-Term SUE continues to be used >50% for SR&ED from acquisition to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition, it qualifies as Second-Term SUE, deeming an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost to be a qualified expenditure.

For Equipment Lease Expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 (reported on Lines 350 and 355 and Box 759 of Form T661), rules differ by overhead method. Under the Traditional Method, leased equipment (including GPOEF) used ≥90% (ASA) of its operating time in SR&ED is 100% allowable as a lease cost, while equipment used <90% of the time in SR&ED (and lease of land) is allowable on a proportional percentage basis as overhead on Line 360 if directly related and incremental. Under the Proxy Method, leased equipment (excluding GPOEF and land) is 100% allowable if used ≥90% (ASA) of its operating time in SR&ED (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)), 50% (1/2) allowable if used primarily (>50% to <90%) of its operating time in SR&ED (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), and 0% allowable if used 50% or less. Operating time is measured across the full taxation year (or for a transition year straddling December 16, 2024, across the period after December 15, 2024), and building rent remains strictly non-allowable unless the building is a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 2903.
6. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Ten Canadian jurisdictions (nine provinces and one territory) offer provincial or territorial R&D tax credits that layer onto the federal SR&ED programme, while Prince Edward Island (PEI), Nunavut, and the Northwest Territories (NWT) do not offer an R&D tax credit. body.text: 6.2 Detailed Analysis of Provincial and Territorial Regimes

In Ontario, corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment that file federal Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 may claim up to three distinct R&D credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario). First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Schedule 566, Schedule 5 Line 468) provides an 8% refundable tax credit (10% prior to June 1, 2016) on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to a $3,000,000 annual expenditure limit (yielding up to $240,000 per year, shared among associated corporations and prorated for short tax years). Following federal Bill C-15, Ontario updated its OITC qualified expenditure rules to include 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (alongside 40% of pre-2014 capital expenditures, while capital expenditures between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024 remain excluded). The $3 million OITC expenditure limit is reduced by two multiplicative phase-out grinds: it phases out linearly when prior-year federal taxable income of the associated group is between $500,000 and $800,000, and independently phases out linearly when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. If both grinds apply (for example, $700,000 prior-year taxable income leaving $1,000,000 of the limit, and $30,000,000 prior-year taxable capital leaving 80% of the band), the two reductions multiply ($1,000,000 × 80% = $800,000 limit, or $64,000 max OITC). Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38–45 / 46–53, Schedule 508, Schedule 5 Line 416) provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit (4.5% prior to June 1, 2016) with no expenditure limit, carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years. Crucially, Ontario treats the OITC as government assistance that reduces the ORDTC base (ORDTC = 3.5% × [Eligible Ontario SR&ED − OITC]). Because both Ontario credits reduce federal qualified expenditures as government assistance, a loss-making corporation may waive the ORDTC under subsection 43(1) (or waive the OITC under subsection 96(14)). Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97, Schedule 568 and Schedule 569, Schedule 5 Line 470) provides a 20% refundable credit on up to $20,000,000 of qualified current expenditures (up to $4,000,000 annual refund, allocated across associated corporations under subsection 38(4) of Ontario Regulation 37/09) incurred under eligible contracts with Ontario Eligible Research Institutes (ERIs)—including Ontario universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, Ontario Centres of Excellence, and Networks of Centres of Excellence.

In Québec, for fiscal years beginning on or before March 25, 2025, the province offered eight separate R&D tax measures: (1) the R&D salary and subcontractor credit (30% for SMEs and 14% for large businesses on 100% of R&D salaries or 50% of subcontracting contracts, subject to a $50,000 SME / $225,000 large business exclusion threshold); (2) the university/public research centre R&D credit (30% SME / 14% large on 80% of contract costs); (3) the pre-competitive research in private partnership credit (30% SME / 14% large on 100% of current expenses and 80% of subcontracts); (4) the research consortium fees credit (30% SME / 14% large on 100% of dues/contributions); (5) the industrial design credit (24% SME / 12% large); (6) the technology adaptation services credit (40% on 80% of CCTT/CLT liaison and transfer fees); and (7–8) the 5-year tax holidays for foreign researchers and foreign experts (100% income deduction for the first two years, then 75%, 50%, and 25%). For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec replaced its fragmented R&D credits with the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), claimed on Revenu Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (supplemented by Form RD-1029.8.EN-T for associated group allocation and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T for pre-commercialization activities). The CRIC provides a 30% fully refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the exclusion threshold and a 20% fully refundable credit on all excess expenditures, with no corporate asset size test. The annual exclusion threshold is the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec basic personal amount for each employee prorated by actual time spent on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization work. Crucially, the CRIC covers both harmonized R&D (reviewed scientifically by the CRA) and eligible pre-commercialization activities conducted in conjunction with Québec R&D (regulatory testing, technological validations, certification studies, product design for aesthetics/functionality/materials, and initial quality control systems), and applies to 100% of employee salaries, 50% of Québec subcontractor contracts, 50% of payments to public research centres, research consortia, or universities, and 100% of capital property acquisition costs (excluding land and buildings, and cannot be combined with the C3i investment tax credit on the same property).

Across Western, Prairie, Atlantic, and Northern Canada, British Columbia (Form T666, Parts 6, sections 97–103 of the British Columbia Income Tax Act) made its 10% SR&ED tax credit permanent in its Budget 2026 (eliminating the former September 1, 2027 expiry date), expanded the 10% refundable credit under section 98 to include Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) alongside CCPCs for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, and linked its expenditure limit to paragraph 127(10.1)(c) of the federal ITA (raising the BC refundable expenditure limit to $6,000,000, with a 10% non-refundable credit on excess expenditures carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years, a 10-year recapture window under sections 102.1–102.6, and a strict 18-month filing deadline). Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (AT1 Schedule 29, Schedule 13, and Form AT4970, governed by sections 26.95–26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and Information Circular IEG-1) provides an 8% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's 2-year prior average base spending and an enhanced 20% refundable payment (8% base plus 12% incremental) on spending above that 2-year average, up to a $4,000,000 annual expenditure cap (maximum $800,000 grant; corporations with $50 million or more in taxable capital are ineligible, and claims are due 15 months after the AT1 filing-due date). Saskatchewan (Schedule 403, sections 63–63.4 of The Income Tax Act, 2000 (Saskatchewan)) announced in its March 18, 2026 Budget an expansion retroactive to December 16, 2024 that includes capital expenditures and doubles the 10% refundable CCPC expenditure limit from $1 million to $2 million, subject to a $1 million combined annual credit cap for refundable and 10% non-refundable credits. Manitoba (Schedule 380, section 7.3 of The Income Tax Act (Manitoba)) offers a 15% credit (including capital and SUE costs, with 100% inclusion for Manitoba educational institution contracts) that is 100% refundable for R&D under contract with a qualifying research institute and 50% refundable (7.5%) / 50% non-refundable (7.5%) for in-house R&D. Finally, New Brunswick (Schedule 360), Nova Scotia (Schedule 340), and Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule 301 / Form T1129) each provide a 15% fully refundable tax credit with no expenditure cap (with Newfoundland and Labrador uniquely not reducing its provincial base by government assistance other than GST/HST input tax credits), while Yukon (Schedule 442) provides a 15% fully refundable credit plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University.
7. Interaction with Government Assistance, Direct Innovation Grants (NRC IRAP, SIF/SRF), and Stacking Math
7.1 Statutory Assistance Reduction Mechanics and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Rule

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the Income Tax Act, government assistance, non-government assistance (amounts included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x)), and contract payments that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year reduce the SR&ED expenditure base. Provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (including provincial super-allowance benefits) and direct government innovation grants (such as NRC IRAP and ISED SIF/SRF contributions) constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9).
As detailed in the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy (Section 4.5), a critical distinction applies when a claimant elects the Proxy Method:

items: Treatment for the Section 37 Deductible Pool: Because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is a notional amount that is not included in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool, the portion of a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit that relates to the PPA does not reduce the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(d). Instead, the portion of the provincial credit attributable to the PPA (as well as any Québec credit earned on R&D-assisting salaries/subcontracts that do not qualify under the federal proxy method) must be included directly in business income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the year received via T2 Schedule 1.

Treatment for Section 127 Qualified Expenditures (ITC Base): Conversely, because the PPA is included in qualified expenditures to calculate the federal ITC, 100% of the provincial or territorial R&D tax credit (including the portion relating to the PPA, whether the provincial credit is refundable or non-refundable) reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18).

Repayment of Assistance: When a claimant subsequently repays government or non-government assistance (Line 560 of Form T661), the Section 37 deductible pool increases to the extent the assistance previously reduced the pool, and the repayment earns an ITC in the year repaid using the original ITC rate; however, ITCs earned on repayments of assistance are non-refundable (carrying back 3 years or forward 20 years).

body.text: 7.2 Step-by-Step Worked Stacking Calculations
To illustrate how provincial and federal credits interact mathematically without simple additive stacking, consider the following scenarios:

First, consider a stand-alone Ontario CCPC with $1,000,000 of current qualified SR&ED expenditures carried on in Ontario (salaries, 55% PPA, materials, and 80% of an arm's-length Ontario contract), prior-year taxable income of $300,000 (below the $500K OITC grind), prior-year taxable capital of $5 million (below the $25M OITC and $15M federal grinds), and no external grants:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566): Applying the 8% refundable OITC rate to the $1,000,000 base yields $80,000 ($1,000,000 × 8%), which is 100% refundable in cash.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508): Because the OITC is government assistance for ORDTC purposes, the ORDTC base is reduced to $1,000,000 − $80,000 = $920,000. Applying the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC rate yields $32,200 ($920,000 × 3.5%), bringing combined Ontario credits to $112,200 (11.22% of the eligible pool).

Federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (Schedule T2SCH31): Both Ontario credits constitute government assistance that reduces the federal qualified expenditure base under subsection 127(18): $1,000,000 − $80,000 − $32,200 = $887,800. Applying the 35% enhanced CCPC rate yields $310,730 ($887,800 × 35%), which is 100% refundable in cash.

Combined Total Recovery: Summing the three credits ($80,000 OITC + $32,200 ORDTC + $310,730 Federal ITC) produces $422,930 (42.29% of the $1,000,000 qualified expenditure pool), of which $390,730 (39.07%) is refunded in cash and $32,200 is a non-refundable Ontario tax credit. When expressed as a percentage of direct T4 SR&ED salary (where $100,000 of direct salary generates $55,000 of PPA to create $155,000 of qualified expenditures), the combined federal and Ontario credits return approximately 61% in cash (from the 8% OITC plus 35% federal ITC) and up to 66% total when including the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC.

body.text: Second, consider the CRA's comparative illustration (from Section 6.10 of the Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy) of a CCPC incurring $100,000 in directly engaged SR&ED salaries, $15,000 in materials, and $50,000 in actual incremental overhead:

items: Under the Traditional Method, allowable SR&ED expenditures added to the Section 37 pool equal $165,000 ($100,000 salary + $15,000 materials + $50,000 actual overhead), PPA is $0, total qualified expenditures equal $165,000, and the federal ITC at 35% equals $57,750.

Under the Proxy Method, allowable SR&ED expenditures added to the Section 37 pool equal $115,000 ($100,000 salary + $15,000 materials, while the $50,000 of actual overhead is deducted as an ordinary business expense), the 55% PPA adds $55,000 ($100,000 × 55%), total qualified expenditures rise to $170,000 ($115,000 + $55,000), and the federal ITC at 35% increases to $59,500.

Similarly, in a multi-component CCPC illustration, a CCPC paying $300,000 in directly engaged SR&ED salaries (which generates $165,000 in PPA at 55%) and $50,000 to an arm's-length Canadian contractor (of which 80%, or $40,000, counts) establishes $505,000 in federal qualified expenditures, earning $176,750 in federal refundable ITCs at 35% before provincial credits.

body.text: 7.3 Coordination with Major Federal Direct Innovation Grants (NRC IRAP and ISED SIF / SRF)

In addition to indirect tax incentives under the SR&ED programme, federal support for business R&D and innovation is delivered through four key direct platforms: the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) / Strategic Response Fund (SRF), the Regional Development Agencies (RDAs), and the Trade Commissioner Service (such as CanExport Innovation).

Administered by the National Research Council of Canada, NRC IRAP provides direct non-repayable contributions and technical advisory support for SME R&D projects up to a $10 million project threshold, with Federal Budget 2026 proposing the renewal of the IRAP Clean Technology Initiative to support the development and commercialisation of clean technologies. For projects exceeding the $10 million IRAP and RDA threshold, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) established the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) in 2017 (consolidating legacy programmes including SADI and AIF) to fund up to 50% of eligible costs across five streams: Stream 1 (R&D and commercialisation), Stream 2 (Firm growth and scale-up), Stream 3 (Investment attraction), Stream 4 (Collaborative industrial research and technology demonstration), and Stream 5 (National innovation ecosystems). Subsequently, ISED transitioned the SIF into the Strategic Response Fund (SRF)—backed by a $5 billion investment plus an additional $1 billion over six years starting in 2028–29 proposed in Budget 2026—which continues to administer all SIF projects and the AI Compute Challenge (supporting domestic AI data centres and compute infrastructure) while expanding support to large-scale R&D, commercialisation, and tariff-adaptation projects larger than $20 million (for contributions of $10 million and above) via unconditionally repayable, conditionally repayable, or non-repayable contributions.

When stacking direct grants (such as NRC IRAP or ISED SIF/SRF contributions) with SR&ED, the grant or repayable government contribution constitutes "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) that must be deducted from the Section 37 pool (Line 429) and from Section 127 qualified expenditures (Line 515). However, under the Proxy Method, receiving an IRAP salary grant does not reduce the gross directly engaged SR&ED salary base (Line 818) used to compute the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount. Consequently, the claimant still generates the full 55% PPA on the gross SR&ED salary before deducting the IRAP grant from total qualified expenditures.

body.text: 8.2 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline (ITA Subsections 37(11) and 127(9)(m))

Under subsection 37(11) (for deducting SR&ED expenditures) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (for earning ITCs), a claimant must file the prescribed forms (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred.

For corporations, because the T2 return filing-due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) is 6 months after the end of the taxation year, the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly 18 months after the end of the taxation year (for example, a corporation with a December 31, 2025 fiscal year-end has a T2 due date of June 30, 2026 and an absolute SR&ED reporting deadline of June 30, 2027). (Note: A corporation exempt from tax that incurs SR&ED expenditures must file Form T661 on or before its 6-month return filing due date or face a late-filing penalty). For individuals and sole proprietors, the SR&ED reporting deadline is 17.5 months after the calendar year-end (June 15 of the second following year).

This reporting deadline is absolute: the CRA cannot by law grant any extension past the 18-month deadline, and general taxpayer relief provisions under subsection 220(3.1) of the ITA cannot be used to revive or accept a late SR&ED claim. Filing estimates, submitting partially completed forms, or sending a letter expressing an "intent to file" does not satisfy the statutory filing requirements. If a claim is filed before the reporting deadline with missing information and the CRA reviews it and notifies the claimant before the deadline, the claimant may submit the missing information only up to the 18-month reporting deadline; if the prescribed project information in Part 2 of Form T661 for specific projects is missing by the deadline, those projects are disallowed while validly completed projects in the claim are accepted. Finally, under paragraph 230(4)(b) of the ITA, claimants must retain all supporting books, records, and contemporaneous technical documentation for at least 6 years from the end of the last taxation year to which the records relate.
8.3 CRA Service Standards, Review Process, Gross Negligence Penalties, and the Four-Step Dispute Resolution Hierarchy

For refundable SR&ED claims, the CRA adheres to three processing service standards (targeted to be met 90% of the time from receipt of a complete claim and tax return; non-refundable claims have no fixed service standard):

items: 60 Calendar Days: Refundable claims accepted as filed without a review.
90 Calendar Days: Refundable claims selected for an expenditure-only review that only include projects granted Pre-Claim Approval.

180 Calendar Days: Refundable claims selected for a technical and/or financial review (including claims with non-pre-approved projects or projects that materially differ from their pre-claim approval).

body.text: If a claimant is filing its first SR&ED claim (or has not filed a claim in the preceding 3 years), the CRA may select the claimant for the mandatory First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS)—an educational meeting conducted after filing that is not an audit, makes no eligibility determinations, releases any expected refund after the meeting, and provides recommendations on identifying eligible work, tracking allowable expenditures, and keeping contemporaneous records for future claims. Conversely, if a claimant knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence files an overstated SR&ED claim, the CRA may assess a Gross Negligence Penalty under subsection 163(2) of the ITA equal to the greater of $100 or 50% of the total of: (a) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (under paragraph 163(2)(a)), plus (b) the entire overstated refundable ITC claimed.

When a claim is selected for a review by an RTA and FR, the review proceeds through three phases—Step 1 (initial telephone contact, identification of review issues, and a written initial contact letter with a meeting agenda and a standard 30-day deadline for pre-meeting information requests), Step 2 (virtual or on-site review meeting, interviews with technical/financial personnel, facility tour, review of dated contemporaneous evidence, and communication of preliminary findings), and Step 3 (issuance of the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report classifying projects as AW [All Work eligible], SW [Some Work eligible], NW [No Work eligible], UN [Unsubstantiated], or AAF [Accepted As Filed], accompanied by a 30-day proposal letter window for the claimant to submit written representations before reassessment). If disagreements arise during or after the review, the CRA's Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns establish a formal four-step dispute resolution hierarchy:

items: Step 1 — Talk to the Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and/or Financial Reviewer (FR): Openly discuss factual or technical concerns and provide clarifying documentation directly to the RTA and FR before the file is closed.

Step 2 — Contact the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM): If unresolved with the reviewers, escalate to the RTM and/or FRM, who review the case facts and perspectives of both parties.

Step 3 — Request an Administrative Review (Form RC532): If concerns remain unresolved after Steps 1 and 2 and the claimant has received the CRA proposal package, the claimant may notify the reviewers within the 30-day proposal period (before the file is closed) and mail Form RC532 to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (Canada Revenue Agency, Business Tax Incentives Directorate, Enterprise Building, 13th Floor, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa, ON K1A 0L5). Forwarded within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director, the Administrative Review is not a second technical review; it determines strictly whether (a) the claimant was given due process and (b) the technical and financial reviews were consistent with current SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures, resulting in either Decision Maintained or Decision Reconsidered.

Step 4 — Formal Notice of Objection and Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada: Within 90 calendar days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, the claimant may file a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch, and if unresolved or confirmed, appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.

Canadian SR&ED administration and audit defence are governed by binding jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA).
