Tax Court of Canada (May 1998, Bowman J.)

Dismissed taxpayer's appeal; confirmed that all five Northwest Hydraulic questions are mandatory legal criteria to separate experimental development from routine engineering.

body.text: 9.1 Detailed Analysis of Key Judicial Precedents
1. Northwest Hydraulic, Consoltex, RIS-Christie, C.W. Agencies, and Jentel Manufacturing: The Binding Five-Part Test

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839; 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC)), Judge Bowman articulated the five criteria that have governed Canadian SR&ED law for nearly three decades: (1) whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; (2) whether the claimant formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty; (3) whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including trained and systematic observation, measurement, experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses; (4) whether the process resulted in a technological advancement; and (5) whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed. While Judge Bowman accepted credible oral testimony in Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen (97 DTC 724 (TCC)), the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 DTC 5087 (FCA)) clarified that contemporaneous documentary evidence of test data and repeatable measurements is indispensable to establish systematic investigation, and subsequently confirmed the five Northwest Hydraulic questions as binding appellate law in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (2001 FCA 393) and Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355).
2. 1726437 Ontario Inc. o/a Airmax Technologies v. The Queen (2012 TCC 376): System Uncertainty and the Informal Procedure Cap

In Airmax Technologies (2012 TCC 376, October 25, 2012), the appellant residential HVAC installer claimed SR&ED expenditures in its 2007 and 2008 taxation years for its "High Static High Velocity Fan Coil System Development" project aimed at developing a compact, quiet (reducing noise from 60 dB to 40 dB), high-velocity heating and cooling system for multi-storey residential townhouses. To overcome uneven vertical heat distribution and high acoustic noise caused by elevated static pressure, Airmax systematically tested and modified four interconnected components: redesigned air diffusers, flexible ductwork with experimental sound-absorbing core perforations (varying hole sizes, counts, and placements), a European boiler adapted to North American domestic hot-water and heating standards, and Korean (Essen Tech) electronically commutated motors (ECMs) programmed with custom control board settings. After conceding $33,650 for an ineligible plastic mould at trial, $387,553 remained in dispute. Justice Hogan ruled that all $387,553 qualified for SR&ED, holding that combining standard technologies in a non-trivial manner created genuine system uncertainty regarding whether the four modified components could function together within target acoustic, pressure, and safety bounds. Furthermore, under subsection 127(26), allowed 2007 expenses that were not paid within 180 days of the 2007 year-end were properly deemed incurred in 2008 for ITC purposes. However, because Airmax had elected the Tax Court's Informal Procedure, Justice Hogan held that under section 18.1 of the Tax Court of Canada Act, paragraph 17(1) of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (Informal Procedure), and Innovations et Intégrations Brassicoles Inc. v. The Queen (2009 FCA 302), the Court's judgment could not increase the aggregate refundable ITC by more than $12,000 for the 2008 taxation year.
3. Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6): Baseline Engineering Knowledge and Post-Hoc Consultant Summaries

In Joel Theatrical Rigging (2017 TCC 6, January 17, 2017), the taxpayer appealed the disallowance of its 2008 and 2009 SR&ED claims for two projects: (1) the 2008 Fire Curtain Project (testing combinations of motors, hydraulic pumps, hoses, and valves using an 800-lb shop weight to achieve a controlled ≤30-second fire curtain descent without counterweights) and (2) the 2009 Manual Override Project (developing a ~$5,000 hand-crank manual override that disengaged a stage curtain's cable drum without losing the limit switch's calibration, where existing high-end systems cost ~$25,000). Only two witnesses testified: the company president (who had a Grade 12 education and 36 years of rigging experience) and the external tax consultant who prepared the Forms T661; no scientist, professional engineer (P.Eng.), or employee with engineering training testified, nor had the company consulted a P.Eng. during the projects. Justice Sommerfeldt dismissed both appeals, holding that: (1) because the taxpayer never consulted a professional engineer, it failed to establish that the problems could not have been readily resolved by standard mechanical/hydraulic engineering knowledge (failing Question 1); (2) experiment summary sheets prepared after the testing by the external tax consultant listing vague "next steps" were not testable scientific hypotheses (failing Question 2); (3) the shop-floor trial-and-error tests did not follow the scientific method (failing Question 3); (4) commercial novelty did not advance general technological understanding (failing Question 4); and (5) contemporaneous records were not kept as work progressed (failing Question 5).
4. Kam-Press Metal Products (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D Inc. (2022 FCA 72): Scientific Method Discipline and Expert Witness Gatekeeping

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2021 FCA 88, affirming 2019 TCC 246), the taxpayer argued that because the words "scientific method" do not appear in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, requiring adherence to the scientific method under Question 3 of Northwest Hydraulic was unlawful. The Federal Court of Appeal rejected this argument and affirmed that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria are binding law. One year later, in National R&D Inc. v. The Queen (2022 FCA 72, affirming 2020 TCC 47), the taxpayer argued that the CRA's August 2021 "Why/How" Guidelines dropped the phrase "scientific method" and that the TCC failed to distinguish between the "scientific method" and the "engineering method". The Federal Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on four grounds: (1) CRA administrative guidance does not bind the courts, and the 2021 "How" requirement still demands underlying experimental rigour and discipline; (2) courts are responsible for giving precision to statutory text; (3) the TCC properly evaluated the scientific method within the taxpayer's business context; and (4) the taxpayer's attempt to prove a distinction between the "engineering method" and "scientific method" by inserting an article into its book of authorities was "an impermissible attempt to establish, through the back door, a fact that should be a matter of evidence at trial". Furthermore, while the TCC permitted the taxpayer's president to testify as a "litigant expert", the FCA upheld the TCC's exclusion of the taxpayer's retained expert witness because the taxpayer had written 65% of the proposed expert's report, rendering it an exercise in advocacy that violated the expert's overriding duty of impartiality to the Court and improperly opined on the legal issue of SR&ED eligibility.
5. CAE Inc. v. His Majesty The King (2022 FCA 178): Concessional Repayable Government Loans as Government Assistance

In CAE Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC 57, affirmed from the bench in CAE Inc. v. His Majesty The King, 2022 FCA 178, October 19, 2022), flight-simulator manufacturer CAE Inc. received unconditionally repayable contributions during its 2012 and 2013 taxation years from Industry Canada (now ISED) under a March 30, 2009 Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative (SADI) agreement. CAE contended that because the SADI loans were unconditionally repayable rather than forgivable grants, they did not constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Applying Canada v. Consumers' Gas Co. ([1987] 2 F.C. 60), Canada v. CCLC Technologies Inc. ([1996] F.C.J. No. 1226), and Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada (2014 FCA 196), both the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal held that because the SADI loan terms were concessional and not strictly commercial, the full amount of the repayable contribution constituted "government assistance" under subsection 127(9)—simultaneously reducing CAE's qualified SR&ED expenditures and ITCs and entering taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the years received. This appellate holding governs all concessional repayable innovation contributions issued under ISED's Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) and Strategic Response Fund (SRF).
